chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, all together from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about a man who said to his wife, 'You are separate from me,' and 'You are free from me,' and 'You are disavowed from me.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is not anything (i.e., it does not constitute a formal divorce).'

key_terms.بَائِنٌ: Separate or distinct; a term often used in divorce contexts but here deemed insufficient for formal divorce.
key_terms.بَرِيئَةٌ: Disavowed or innocent; implying the husband is free from obligations to her or vice versa.
key_terms.خَلِيَّةٌ: Free or exempt; implying freedom from the husband's authority or bond.
key_terms.لَيْسَ بِشَيْءٍ: It is nothing; a legal ruling indicating the utterance has no legal effect in this context.

ai.seo_question: Do phrases like 'you are separate from me' or 'you are free from me' count as divorce in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies that the phrases 'bain' (severed), 'khalliyyah' (free/disengaged), and 'baree'ah' (innocent/cleared) constitute mere expressions of separation or affection rather than formal talaq, preserving the marital bond. In Shia jurisprudence, this highlights the principle of 'al-ibtal' (non-effectiveness) for ambiguous utterances unless explicitly intended as divorce, distinguishing them from the clear 'zahir' forms. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on linguistic precision and the husband's intent in marital dissolution.
